title: Barriers to entry by ANZSIC 2006 class
description: Each ANZSIC class is put in one of six groups, after Grattan Institute's sector groups (Minifie, Chisholm and Percival 2017, Competition in Australia: too little of a good thing?, section 1.3 and Figures 1.3, 4.4 and 5.2). Where Grattan names a sector, its class follows Grattan ('grattan' gives Grattan's label). Elsewhere the division default applies, with the exceptions listed here, each with a reason. Grattan's own allocation used IBISWorld industries and its judgement of cost structures and regulation, and was 'inherently subjective' (its footnote 9); so is this one. The finest code listed wins: a class entry overrides a group or subdivision entry, which overrides the division default.

natural_monopoly.label: Natural monopolies
natural_monopoly.about: One network usually serves each market, because building a second would waste money: electricity and gas networks, airports, ports, rail freight, pipelines and the fixed-line phone network.

scale_economies.label: Scale economies
scale_economies.about: Big firms have much lower costs than small ones, so a few firms hold most of the market: supermarkets, fuel and liquor retailing, airlines, mobile and internet services, broadcasting and pathology.

heavy_regulation.label: Heavy regulation
heavy_regulation.about: Rules limit who can operate, or cost small firms much more to follow: banks, insurance, pharmacies, gambling, taxis and residential aged care.

low_barriers.label: Low barriers
low_barriers.about: The rest of the private businesses that mostly sell within Australia, where new firms can start up and compete relatively easily.

tradeable.label: Tradeable
tradeable.about: Farms, mines and factories, which compete with imports and exports. Grattan left them out of its analysis.

public.label: Mostly public
public.about: Services mostly run by governments or not-for-profits, such as public administration, schools, hospitals and water. Grattan left them out of its analysis.

codes.note: Not named by Grattan; gas distribution through mains is a network natural monopoly, like electricity distribution (Grattan's footnote 10).
The ATO publishes rail freight and rail passenger transport only together, and only in its group table (company income is mostly rail freight; passenger rail is mostly state-run).

Grattan's toll road operators cannot be shown separately. ANZSIC 5299 holds toll road, toll bridge, container terminal and railway station operation together with freight brokerage, weighbridges and driving services (ABS class description): most of its businesses are small transport-support firms (entry about 17% a year for employing businesses, against 6-9% for the network classes), and the large toll road operators are largely trusts (stapled securities), outside company tax statistics, where the class's equity was negative in two of five years. So the class stays with low barriers.
In ATO data most mobile network operators also report under this class, so it holds most of Grattan's 'Wireless Telecom.' as well.
One ANZSIC class for domestic and international air transport; Grattan put international airlines with low barriers.
Grattan's 'Delivery Services' could be postal, courier or both; both are put here.
